<reason>Side A (PRO) won a closely fought, high-quality exchange. A built a coherent portfolio/pipeline case (asymmetric upside with capped downside, franchise degradation, talent development) and then escalated into a decisive meta-argument: CON conceded originals renew the slate, franchises degrade, and mega-sequels can be ruinous, while every CON remedy — better evaluation, selective originals, microbudgets, acquisitions — describes what studios already claim to do while the mid-budget tier collapsed. B's best responses were real: the burden framing (renewal matters ≠ this tier deserves more dollars), accurate corrections of PRO's examples (Paranormal was microbudget; Harry Potter was an adaptation), and the sharp final parry that a bigger allocation "forces expenditure, not renewal." But B's answer to A's strongest pressure question — what force actually makes evaluation reform happen under incentives that reward predictability — was circular ("the studio's interest in owning its next property"), and B never supplied the loss-comparison it demanded of A, while A at least gave the direction (one franchise misfire erases the search cost of many modest originals) plus the asymmetry that makes higher spending robust to imperfect selection. Both sides followed format, answered pressure directly with A1/A2, and avoided fake precision; B was slightly more epistemically careful, A was more decisive and made the debate easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Q1 ("what force makes your evaluation fix happen?") against B's Rebuttal 2 A1 answer. B could only cite the studio's own interest in owning future properties — an interest that demonstrably did not prevent the hollowing out A documented — while A's follow-up closing ("CON's fix is the status quo wearing a reformer's clothes") converted that exchange into the debate's decisive clash.</best_rebuttal>
